title: Kernel hint layer and fragment-stitcher for paged-attention adaptive backpressure
creator: Aisha Banerjee
description:
Problem: Paged attention workloads suffer intermittent decode stalls caused by mismatched kernel placement and fragmented KV pages. When a decode wave requests sparse KV fragments across shards, the runtime currently issues many small kernel launches with suboptimal kernel variant selection, which increases per-token latency and wastes GPU occupancy.

Goal: Implement a lightweight kernel-hinting layer combined with a fragment-stitcher that: (1) aggregates nearby KV fragments into stitch candidates at prefill time, (2) provides a hint score to the kernel selector to prefer compact kernels or fused microkernels when beneficial, and (3) applies adaptive backpressure when prefill load threatens tail SLOs.

Acceptance criteria: 
- End-to-end p90 token latency for the internal e2e-bench workload decreases by >= 12% on mixed sparse-hot traces.
- Per-token GPU utilization improves (measured on perf dashboard) without increasing p99 latency by more than 3%.
- New hinting layer has feature flag and telemetry hooks (hint hit/miss ratio, stitch success rate).
- No regression on dense decoding traces (verify with unit and integration benchmarks).

Design notes: 
- Kernel hint layer: shallow API between prefill scheduler and kernel-selector that carries "compactness" and "stride" scores computed from fragment metadata. Hints are advisory; selector falls back to cost-model when unavailable.
- Fragment-stitcher: background coalescer at prefill that attempts to merge adjacent fragments (same shard, contiguous token span) into temporary stitched descriptors for kernel invocation. Stitching is memory-safe: stitched descriptors reference original pages and have a short TTL.
- Adaptive backpressure: a credit-based controller that throttles new prefill requests for tenants when the hint-layer reports > 60% hint-misses and decode queues exceed soft limit. Uses exponentially-smoothed metrics to avoid oscillation.
- Safety: stitcher never writes to KV pages; it's a descriptor-level operation. Eviction/invalidation is coordinated via a lightweight lease check to avoid races.

Trade-offs considered: 
- Eager stitching reduces kernel-launch overhead but may increase bookkeeping overhead and temporary descriptor memory. We bias toward low-latency workloads by making stitching opt-in per-tenant and bounded by a global descriptor cap.
- Hinting is advisory to avoid coupling selector correctness to heuristics. We accept occasional suboptimal choices if the cost-model disagrees; telemetry will guide later policy changes.

Testing & rollout plan: 
1) Unit tests for stitcher invariants (no writes, TTL expiry, lease checks).
2) Microbench on small instance to validate kernel-launch reduction (target >= 25% fewer launches on sparse traces).
3) Canary rollout behind feature flag for 5% of hosted traffic (low priority tenants) with aggressive telemetry (hint hit/miss, stitch rate, token latencies).
4) Expand to Dedicated clusters after 2-weeks of stable canary with performance gains.

Monitoring: Connect metrics to console-perf dashboard: stitch_success_rate, hint_advice_rate, kernel_variant_change_count, prefill_backpressure_events, tenant_throttles. Create alert when stitch_success_rate < 5% for >30m and p95 latency regresses.

Docs/links: Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Kernel+Hint+and+Fragment+Stitcher
Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1482
Perf dashboard (internal): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv-prefill/paged-attention-prefill?view=kernel-hints

Longer-term ideas: 
- Integrate hint signals into the ML-based kernel-cost model.
- Opportunistically materialize stitched pages for very hot spans (requires eviction protocol).
